cues.text: Let's turn now to additional design patterns and engineering practice.
This section pulls together several ideas that students often blur together, so we will separate them carefully.
Begin with four terms that sound similar but answer different questions.
First, client-server.
Client-server describes interaction and distribution: it tells you how parts of a system talk to one another and where they are placed.
One side requests, the other side serves.
Second, MVC, which stands for Model-View-Controller.
MVC separates presentation responsibilities.
It is about keeping the way something is shown to the user apart from the other concerns of the application.
Third, layered architecture.
A layered architecture organises logical responsibilities.
Think of it as stacking the system by the kind of job each part does, so that each layer has a clear purpose.
Fourth, microservices.
Microservices define deployment and domain boundaries.
Each service is drawn around a business domain and can be deployed as its own unit.

So, to keep them apart: client-server is about interaction and distribution, MVC is about presentation responsibilities, layered architecture is about logical responsibilities, and microservices are about deployment and domain boundaries.
These are not four competing answers to one question.
They address different questions.
Now a practical consequence.
A layered modular monolith can be simpler to operate than distributed services for a small team.
A monolith is deployed as one unit, and being layered and modular means it still has internal structure.
The source's point is that, for a small team, this can be simpler to run than a set of distributed services.
Notice the qualification: it says "can be", not "always is".
Next, event-driven integration.
When you choose it, you should document seven things.
One, the event schema, meaning the structure of the event.
Two, ownership, meaning who is responsible for the event.
Three, delivery guarantees, meaning what promises are made about delivery.
Four, retry and deduplication, meaning how failed deliveries are tried again and how duplicates are handled.
Five, dead-letter handling, meaning what happens to events that cannot be processed.
And six, observability, meaning how you can see and monitor what is happening.
That is six items; to restate the list in order: event schema, ownership, delivery guarantees, retry and deduplication, dead-letter handling, and observability.
Retry and deduplication are written together in the source, so I have treated them as one item.
Alongside that, use explicit service contracts and migration compatibility.
A service contract states clearly what a service offers and expects, and migration compatibility means changes and migrations should remain compatible with that contract.
Now, performance.
When you have a performance concern, follow a disciplined sequence.
First, establish a representative baseline, so you know what normal looks like under realistic conditions.
Second, profile to find the bottleneck.
Third, change one factor only.
Fourth, retest.
Fifth, compare, and the comparison covers correctness and resource use, not just speed.
Changing one factor at a time is what lets you say which change caused which effect.
Finally, error handling.
A useful error-handling policy distinguishes three kinds of problem.
One, expected validation errors, such as input that does not meet the rules.
Two, temporary dependency failure, where something your system relies on is briefly unavailable.
Three, unexpected internal defects, which are genuine bugs.
The policy then has four practices.
Provide safe user-facing errors, so users see messages that are helpful and do not reveal internals.
Log correlation IDs, so that related log entries for one request can be tied together.
Alert on meaningful failures, rather than on every minor event.
And never expose credentials or stack traces publicly.

To recap the chapter: separate the four architectural concerns, document event-driven integration fully, measure performance changes one factor at a time, and handle errors by category while keeping sensitive detail out of public view.
